sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: ATOM3D evaluates predictions from molecular structures using eight separate tasks. It supplies task-specific reference labels and partitions, ranging from random small molecules to held-out protein families and future structure-prediction targets. Each task has its own metric and representation-matched baseline; the suite is not a single universal structure score.

instructions.title: Compute embeddings
instructions.code:
import os, sys
current_path = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
parent_dir = os.path.dirname(current_path)
sys.path.append(parent_dir)
from model.utrlm.modeling_utrlm import UtrLmModel
from tokenizer.tokenization_opensource import OpenRnaLMTokenizer

tokenizer = OpenRnaLMTokenizer.from_pretrained('./checkpoint/opensource/utr-lm-mrl', model_max_length=1026, padding_side="right", use_fast=True,)
model = UtrLmModel.from_pretrained('./checkpoint/opensource/utr-lm-mrl')     
sequences = ["AUUCCGAUUCCGAUUCCG"]
output = tokenizer.batch_encode_plus(sequences, return_tensors="pt", padding="longest", max_length = 1026, truncation=True)
input_ids = output["input_ids"]
attention_mask = output["attention_mask"]

embedding = model(input_ids=input_ids,attention_mask=attention_mask)[0] # shape [bz,length, hidden_size]
print(embedding.shape)

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: BEELINE evaluates gene regulatory network inference from single-cell expression. It runs inference algorithms on synthetic, curated-model and experimental datasets, then compares ranked predicted edges with known or constructed reference networks. Pseudotime requirements and reference-network reliability are part of each evaluation.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: BEND asks whether DNA representations support realistic human-genome annotation across short and long contexts. Frozen embeddings feed a small CNN for supervised tasks, while variant-effect prediction compares reference and alternate embeddings without fitting a task predictor. Whole-chromosome or sequence-identity partitions and specialist baselines make the tested capability explicit.

run_guide.summary: Run the official gene-finding downstream example with BEND's own ResNet-LM and AWD-LSTM embedders, fetching only the gene-finding inputs. This is one BEND task, not the entire suite.
prerequisites: Git and a conda environment with Python 3.10; the README recommends this Python version.
curl and wget on the PATH: the download step uses curl, and BEND's embedders call wget to fetch their checkpoints.
About 3.7 GB of disk: 3.5 GB for the gene-finding inputs and 166 MB for the two checkpoints, plus room for the embeddings.
Internet access to the official data host, sid.erda.dk. Preserve the downloaded data directory structure.

steps.title: Check out the reviewed code
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/frederikkemarin/BEND.git
cd BEND
git checkout --detach 58ad41011125cfca339d511e9b8eb536a54b582a
steps.explanation: The clone command comes from the README; the detached checkout selects commit 58ad410, the first revision with working checkpoint links (BEND PR #79).
steps.source_locator: README.md at 58ad410, lines 39-40; pinned repository revision

steps.title: Install and download the gene-finding data
steps.shell:
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .
S=https://sid.erda.dk/share_redirect/aNQa0Oz2lY
mkdir -p data/genomes data/gene_finding
for f in GRCh38.primary_assembly.genome.fa GRCh38.primary_assembly.genome.fa.fai; do
  curl -fL -o "data/genomes/$f" "$S/data/genomes/$f"
done
for f in gene_finding.bed gene_finding.hdf5; do
  curl -fL -o "data/gene_finding/$f" "$S/data/gene_finding/$f"
done
steps.explanation: Run within the prepared Python 3.10 environment. From commit 58ad410 requirements.txt includes lxml, h5py and pysam, which earlier revisions lacked. The curl loop replaces python scripts/download_bend.py, which downloads the whole share (7,251,859,341 bytes listed on 2026-11-17). Gene finding reads only the GRCh38 reference and the gene_finding bed and hdf5 files, 3,509,054,493 bytes with the index. The README asks for the data folder structure to be kept, which these paths do.
steps.source_locator: README.md at 58ad410, lines 41-43 and 48; requirements.txt at 58ad410, lines 14-19; conf/embedding/embed.yaml at 58ad410, lines 39 and 106-109

steps.title: Precompute the gene-finding embeddings
steps.shell: python scripts/precompute_embeddings.py model=resnetlm,awdlstm task=gene_finding
steps.explanation: Adapted from the README example, with the task list narrowed to gene_finding because only those inputs are fetched. When pretrained_models/convnet/ or pretrained_models/awd_lstm/ is missing, ConvNetEmbedder and AWDLSTMEmbedder download the checkpoints with wget from ERDA share aNQa0Oz2lY. The resnetlm configuration loads pretrained_models/convnet, which the maintainer confirmed holds the paper's dilated ResNet; the resnetlm folder on the share is empty. To fetch the checkpoints ahead of time, call bend.utils.download.download_model('convnet', destination_dir='./pretrained_models/convnet/') and the same for 'awd_lstm'. With its default destination_dir the function writes the files directly into ./pretrained_models/, where the configuration does not look.
steps.source_locator: README.md at 58ad410, line 58; conf/embedding/embed.yaml at 58ad410, lines 40 and 77-82; commit 58ad410, bend/utils/download.py and bend/utils/embedders.py

steps.explanation: Run after gene-finding embeddings are present in data/gene_finding/<embedder>/. Task-specific Hydra configuration supplies the data, model and evaluation settings.

instructions.title: Schedule prepared scoring with site-specific resources
instructions.code:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# Set these for your cluster; no performance or resource estimate is implied.
: "${REWIRE_ACCOUNT:?Set your Slurm account}"
: "${REWIRE_PARTITION:?Set your Slurm partition}"
: "${REWIRE_CPUS:?Set the requested CPU count}"
: "${REWIRE_MEMORY:?Set the requested memory}"
: "${REWIRE_WALLTIME:?Set the requested time limit}"
: "${REWIRE_JOB_ROOT:?Set a shared absolute directory with prepared data and SIF}"
export REWIRE_JOB_ROOT
sbatch --account="$REWIRE_ACCOUNT" --partition="$REWIRE_PARTITION" \
  --cpus-per-task="$REWIRE_CPUS" --mem="$REWIRE_MEMORY" \
  --time="$REWIRE_WALLTIME" --export=ALL <<'REWIRE_JOB'
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$REWIRE_JOB_ROOT"
mkdir -p runs
apptainer run --cleanenv --containall \
  --bind "$PWD/prepared-dart-task1:/prepared:ro" \
  --bind "$PWD/predictions:/predictions:ro" \
  --bind "$PWD/runs:/outputs:rw" \
  rewirebench-core.sif evaluate \
  --prepared /prepared --predictions /predictions/predictions.json \
  --output /outputs/dart-task1-rescore
REWIRE_JOB

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: FLIP evaluates sequence-to-fitness models under protein-engineering distribution shifts. It separates landscapes from their partitions: the same assay can test random interpolation, higher mutation counts, higher fitness or transfer across sequence groups. Comparisons are meaningful within the same landscape and split.

sections.body: FLIP2 extends protein fitness testing to enzyme activity, spectral properties, hydrophobic-core effects and protein interactions. Its partitions hold out mutation positions, mutation numbers, fitness ranges or parent sequences. Simple one-hot ridge models and pretrained versus randomly initialized networks make the baseline comparison interpretable.

instructions.title: Score supplied keyed predictions

import rewirebench
prepared = rewirebench.prepare(
    'flip2-fitness-v1', source='flip2-data', output='prepared-flip2', dataset='flip2-rhomax-by-wild-type', limit=8
)

    prepared, 'predictions.json', output='results-flip2-rescore',
    model={'name': 'My private model', 'training_overlap': 'Unreported'},

cd rewire-benchmarks
git checkout --detach fcccbbcdbe3d5cd64a1a312d536615273320f7b4

instructions.title: Schedule prepared scoring with site-specific resources
instructions.code:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# Set these for your cluster; no performance or resource estimate is implied.
: "${REWIRE_ACCOUNT:?Set your Slurm account}"
: "${REWIRE_PARTITION:?Set your Slurm partition}"
: "${REWIRE_CPUS:?Set the requested CPU count}"
: "${REWIRE_MEMORY:?Set the requested memory}"
: "${REWIRE_WALLTIME:?Set the requested time limit}"
: "${REWIRE_JOB_ROOT:?Set a shared absolute directory with prepared data and SIF}"
export REWIRE_JOB_ROOT
sbatch --account="$REWIRE_ACCOUNT" --partition="$REWIRE_PARTITION" \
  --cpus-per-task="$REWIRE_CPUS" --mem="$REWIRE_MEMORY" \
  --time="$REWIRE_WALLTIME" --export=ALL <<'REWIRE_JOB'
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$REWIRE_JOB_ROOT"
mkdir -p runs
apptainer run --cleanenv --containall \
  --bind "$PWD/prepared-flip2:/prepared:ro" \
  --bind "$PWD/predictions:/predictions:ro" \
  --bind "$PWD/runs:/outputs:rw" \
  rewirebench-core.sif evaluate \
  --prepared /prepared --predictions /predictions/predictions.json \
  --output /outputs/flip2-rescore
REWIRE_JOB

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: GlycanML evaluates taxonomy, immunogenicity, glycosylation type and protein–glycan interaction. Glycans are encoded as IUPAC sequences or graphs. Structural motif clusters define the first three task partitions, whereas interaction prediction holds out protein sequence clusters and predicts a transformed fluorescence binding signal.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: GUE combines genome sequence classification tasks with supplied partitions and task-specific metrics. Models are fine-tuned on labelled training examples, selected with validation data and scored on test data. Random partitions occur in the suite, so a high score does not automatically demonstrate transfer to unrelated genomes.

diagram.title: Evaluation procedure
steps: Allowed inputs: DNA sequences from the benchmark archive, separate from model-pretraining data.

Splits: Separate train/validation/test files and counts are defined per dataset. The yeast epigenetic tasks use an 8:1:1 random split; source-derived regulatory and viral tasks retain their own documented partitions. There is no universal chromosome holdout across GUE.
Metrics: GUE uses Matthews correlation coefficient for the regulatory classification tasks and F1 for COVID variant classification; the exact task metric is tabulated in the dataset appendix.

import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("zhihan1996/DNABERT-2-117M", trust_remote_code=True)

instructions.title: Evaluate on GUE
instructions.code:
export DATA_PATH=/path/to/GUE #(e.g., /home/user)
cd finetune

# Evaluate DNABERT-2 on GUE
sh scripts/run_dnabert2.sh DATA_PATH

# Evaluate DNABERT (e.g., DNABERT with 3-mer) on GUE
# 3 for 3-mer, 4 for 4-mer, 5 for 5-mer, 6 for 6-mer
sh scripts/run_dnabert1.sh DATA_PATH 3

# Evaluate Nucleotide Transformers on GUE
# 0 for 500m-1000g, 1 for 500m-human-ref, 2 for 2.5b-1000g, 3 for 2.5b-multi-species
sh scripts/run_nt.sh DATA_PATH 0

profile.summary: HEST-Benchmark tests prediction of gene expression from histological image representations.
profile.summary_source_locator: Pinned README: HEST-Benchmark overview; evaluation notes

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: HEST-Benchmark connects histology patches to spatially measured gene expression. A patch encoder supplies features to a regression model, which predicts highly variable genes. Patient-stratified folds evaluate transfer between individuals, and correlation is summarized across those folds.
sections.source_locator: Sections 5.1–5.2; Appendix Table A11

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The released MassSpecGym MS/MS/molecule dataset, with task-specific inputs and candidate sets. MCES molecular clusters are grouped into fixed training, validation and test folds, stratified by acquisition metadata. Cross-fold molecular bond-edit distance is at least 10; all spectra follow the assigned molecular fold. Task evaluators distinguish molecular exact match/structural similarity, candidate-retrieval hit rate and spectrum similarity. These are separate readouts, not interchangeable scores. Maximum common edge subgraph (MCES) clustering keeps molecules connected by a bond-edit distance below 10 in the same fold. The split additionally balances instrument, collision-energy, adduct and molecule-frequency metadata; this is stronger than simply separating 2D InChIKeys.

steps.title: Run the documented CPU training and test example
steps.shell:
cat > massspecgym_retrieval_example.py <<'PY'
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import pytorch_lightning as pl
from pytorch_lightning import Trainer

from massspecgym.data import RetrievalDataset, MassSpecDataModule
from massspecgym.data.transforms import SpecTokenizer, MolFingerprinter
from massspecgym.models.base import Stage
from massspecgym.models.retrieval.base import RetrievalMassSpecGymModel

class MyDeepSetsRetrievalModel(RetrievalMassSpecGymModel):
    def __init__(
        self,
        hidden_channels: int = 128,
        out_channels: int = 4096,  # fingerprint size
        *args,
        **kwargs
    ):
        """Implement your architecture."""
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)

        self.phi = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, hidden_channels),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_channels, hidden_channels),
            nn.ReLU(),
        )
        self.rho = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(hidden_channels, hidden_channels),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_channels, out_channels),
            nn.Sigmoid()
        )

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """Implement your prediction logic."""
        x = self.phi(x)
        x = x.sum(dim=-2)  # sum over peaks
        x = self.rho(x)
        return x

    def step(
        self, batch: dict, stage: Stage
    ) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
        """Implement your custom logic of using predictions for training and inference."""
        # Unpack inputs
        x = batch["spec"]  # input spectra
        fp_true = batch["mol"]  # true fingerprints
        cands = batch["candidates"]  # candidate fingerprints concatenated for a batch
        batch_ptr = batch["batch_ptr"]  # number of candidates per sample in a batch

        # Predict fingerprint
        fp_pred = self.forward(x)

        # Calculate loss
        loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(fp_true, fp_pred)

        # Calculate final similarity scores between predicted fingerprints and retrieval candidates
        fp_pred_repeated = fp_pred.repeat_interleave(batch_ptr, dim=0)
        scores = nn.functional.cosine_similarity(fp_pred_repeated, cands)

        return dict(loss=loss, scores=scores)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Init hyperparameters
    n_peaks = 60
    fp_size = 4096
    batch_size = 32

    # Load dataset
    dataset = RetrievalDataset(
        spec_transform=SpecTokenizer(n_peaks=n_peaks),
        mol_transform=MolFingerprinter(fp_size=fp_size),
    )

    # Init data module
    data_module = MassSpecDataModule(
        dataset=dataset,
        batch_size=batch_size,
        num_workers=4
    )

    # Init model
    model = MyDeepSetsRetrievalModel(out_channels=fp_size)

    # Init trainer
    trainer = Trainer(accelerator="cpu", devices=1, max_epochs=5)

    # Train
    trainer.fit(model, datamodule=data_module)

    # Test
    trainer.test(model, datamodule=data_module)
PY
python massspecgym_retrieval_example.py

instructions.title: Embed and evaluate
instructions.code:
import torch

import mrna_bench as mb
from mrna_bench.embedder import DatasetEmbedder
from mrna_bench.linear_probe import LinearProbeBuilder

device = torch.device("cuda")

dataset = mb.load_dataset("go-mf")
model = mb.load_model("Orthrus", "orthrus-large-6-track", device)

embedder = DatasetEmbedder(model, dataset)
embeddings = embedder.embed_dataset()
embeddings = embeddings.detach().cpu().numpy()

prober = (LinearProbeBuilder(dataset)
    .fetch_embedding_by_embedding_instance("orthrus-large-6", embeddings)
    .build_splitter("homology", species="human", eval_all_splits=False)
    .build_evaluator("multilabel")
    .set_target("target")
    .build()
)

metrics = prober.run_linear_probe(2541)
print(metrics)

profile.summary: ProteinGym separates experimental variant-effect and clinical annotation tasks under supervised and zero-shot regimes.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: DMS assays and human clinical variants, with substitution and indel collections kept separate. Five-fold random, contiguous-position and modulo-position cross-validation are separate supervised DMS regimes. The original clinical analysis uses available ClinVar labels with explicit overlap warnings; zero-shot scoring does not fit on assay labels. Zero-shot DMS: Spearman, NDCG, AUC, MCC and top-K recall; supervised DMS: Spearman/MSE; clinical: AUC. Aggregation first groups assays by UniProt ID, then averages functional categories. Supervised DMS evaluations distinguish five-fold random, contiguous-position and modulo-position partitions. The original clinical benchmark explicitly warns that supervised methods may overlap ClinVar labels and that population-frequency training can leak information into benign-variant evaluation.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: In the original supervised single-substitution analysis, random folds assign mutants, contiguous folds group sequence positions into segments, and modulo folds assign positions by remainder. Five folds are usual; the paper excepts F7YBW8_MESOW and SPG1_STRSG, which have four mutated positions. The pinned supervised scorer uses random splits only for indels; substitution schemes remain separate. Zero-shot scoring does not fit assay labels.

profile.summary: scIB is an atlas-level single-cell integration benchmark study covering RNA, chromatin-accessibility and simulated datasets. It compares batch removal with preservation of biological variation. The scib Python package and scib-pipeline implement its evaluation workflow.
profile.summary_source_locator: Primary paper Abstract; Results: Single-cell integration benchmarking (scIB), Figure 1 and Table 1; Methods: Datasets and preprocessing; Code availability. Pinned scib README lines 7-33, 62-100.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The published scIB study compares integration methods on 13 atlas-level tasks spanning RNA, chromatin-accessibility and simulated data. Each task defines its batches and biological annotations. Four preprocessing choices combine scaled or unscaled values with full features or highly variable features for the RNA comparisons. Metrics measure batch correction and biological conservation separately. Label-assisted methods must retain that additional-input distinction. The scib package computes metrics and the separate scib-pipeline coordinates integrations; neither software package is itself a fixed dataset or a universal train/test split.

instructions.code:
from tdc import BenchmarkGroup
group = BenchmarkGroup(name = 'ADMET_Group', path = 'data/')
predictions_list = []

for seed in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
    benchmark = group.get('Caco2_Wang')
    # all benchmark names in a benchmark group are stored in group.dataset_names
    predictions = {}
    name = benchmark['name']
    train_val, test = benchmark['train_val'], benchmark['test']
    train, valid = group.get_train_valid_split(benchmark = name, split_type = 'default', seed = seed)

        # --------------------------------------------- #
        #  Train your model using train, valid, test    #
        #  Save test prediction in y_pred_test variable #
        # --------------------------------------------- #

profile.summary: The read classification part of Hall and Coin 2024: label each non-human read in a sputum-like metagenome as Mycobacterium tuberculosis or not. Kraken2 and minimap2 are each run with three databases, standard and custom, on simulated and artificial real Nanopore and Illumina data. It is for people building culture-free tuberculosis sequencing pipelines who need to choose a classifier and database, including on a laptop.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Classification of Mycobacterium reads

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How accurately each tool and database labels reads as M. tuberculosis, with as few false positives and false negatives as possible, and what it costs in runtime and memory. The authors frame this as a step toward sequencing directly from sputum, where contamination is higher than in culture.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Discussion

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Simulated reads mimic sputum: 46% bacteria, 46% human, 6% M. tuberculosis complex and 1% each virus and NTM, 4.5 gigabases of Nanopore and 0.9 of Illumina. The artificial real set combines real reads from three 1000 Genomes people, an M. tuberculosis isolate and the ZymoBIOMICS HMW standard, so each read's true taxon is known. Classification uses the non-human reads left after host removal: 100,733 simulated Nanopore reads, 1,417,015 simulated Illumina pairs, 915,209 real Nanopore reads and 21,172,961 real Illumina pairs. Simulation genomes were kept out of the custom kraken Mycobacterium database.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Generating in silico metagenomic reads; Creation of an artificial real metagenomic dataset; Results

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Kraken2 uses the standard, standard-8 and a custom Mycobacterium database; minimap2 uses an M. tuberculosis database, the Clockwork decontamination database and a Mycobacterium genus database. A true positive is an M. tuberculosis read classified as M. tuberculosis. Each configuration is scored by sensitivity, specificity and Youden's index with Wilson score 95% intervals, plus mean runtime and peak memory over 10 runs with 4 threads.

attributes.task: Species-level presence detection and relative abundance estimation in mock microbial communities
attributes.source_locator: Tables 1-4; Methods 'Detection metrics' and 'Relative abundance estimates'

profile.summary: This is a benchmark of taxonomic classification and profiling tools, not of models. Eleven methods, five of them written for long reads, were run on public mock community datasets sequenced with PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore and Illumina, where the species present and their intended abundances are known. Each method is scored on how many reads it uses, how precisely and completely it detects the known species, and how close its abundance estimates are to the manufacturer's specification.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and methods

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Three things per method and dataset. Read utilisation: what fraction of the reads the method assigns. Detection: precision, recall and F-score for the known species or genera, where a true positive is a mock community taxon whose read count passes a threshold and a false positive is any taxon not in the community. Abundance accuracy: the L1 distance between estimated and theoretical abundances, with a chi-squared goodness of fit test against the manufacturer's specification.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Detection metrics and Relative abundance estimates

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The datasets are public, empirical sequencing runs of commercial mock communities, chosen over simulations because simulations do not capture real error profiles, read length spread or extraction and library effects. They include a PacBio HiFi run of ATCC MSA-1003 (20 bacterial species in staggered abundances from 18% down to 0.02%; 2.4 million HiFi reads, median length 8.3 kb, 20.54 Gb) and a PacBio HiFi run of ZymoBIOMICS D6331 (17 species including one archaeon and two yeasts, staggered from 14% down to 0.0001%; 1.9 million reads, median 8.1 kb, 17.99 Gb), plus Oxford Nanopore R10 and Q20 runs of ZymoBIOMICS D6300 and Illumina runs of both communities. The truth is the species list and the manufacturer's stated genomic DNA abundances.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Mock community datasets; Relative abundance estimates

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Presence or absence is scored against a minimum percentage of the dataset's total reads, not a fixed read count, because the datasets differ in size. Three thresholds are used: 0.001% (mild), 0.1% (moderate) and 1% (heavy); Table 3 gives the resulting read counts per dataset, for example 24 reads at 0.001% and 24,190 at 1% for HiFi ATCC MSA-1003. Scoring is done at both species and genus level. Abundances are normalised with all false positives summed into an 'Other' category, which is compared against a theoretical abundance of zero, and the chi-squared test uses a Bonferroni correction over the 11 methods, so the altered alpha is 0.0045.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Detection metrics; Relative abundance estimates; Table 3

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The paper prints the general command for each method, so a reader can repeat the analysis on the same public datasets. Kraken2 2.1.1 with the pre-built PlusPF database writes a kreport per sample; Bracken 2.6.0 then produces species-level abundances from that kreport. The other methods each have their own commands and databases in the same section. The kreport outputs, notebooks and results files are on the Open Science Framework project bqtdu.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Profiling method commands; Availability of data and materials; OSF record

run_guide.summary: Download one mock community dataset and run the paper's own Kraken2 and Bracken commands on it.
prerequisites: Kraken2 version 2.1.1 and Bracken version 2.6.0, the versions the paper used.

steps.title: Get a dataset

# HiFi ATCC MSA-1003: NCBI PRJNA546278, run SRX6095783
# download with your preferred SRA client and convert to SAMPLE.fasta
steps.explanation: The paper names the accession for each dataset in its availability statement but gives no download command, so this step is an instruction rather than a command.

steps.title: Classify the reads with Kraken2
steps.shell: kraken2 --db PlusPF --threads 24 –report SAMPLE.kreport.txt SAMPLE.fasta > SAMPLE.kraken
steps.explanation: The paper's Kraken2 command, copied as printed. Note that the report flag as printed in the article uses a non-standard dash character.

steps.explanation: The paper's Bracken command, which reads the Kraken2 report and gives species-level abundances.

profile.summary: A clinical comparison of two metagenomic workflows for detecting microbes in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid: short-read sequencing on MGI and host-depleted nanopore sequencing (HD-ONT). On 62 BALF specimens, each workflow's organism calls are scored against culture, clinical microbiological tests and a composite reference standard by positive and negative percent agreement. It is for clinical microbiology labs weighing short-read against rapid nanopore metagenomics for pneumonia diagnostics.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Clinical performance evaluation

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether each sequencing workflow finds the organisms that reference methods find in a patient's BALF, and how many extra organisms it reports. The paper also studies mock communities, but the store's protocols cover only the 62 clinical specimens.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Study design

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Residual BALF specimens with traceable culture results were sequenced with the MGI short-read workflow (MGISEQ-200, single-end 50 bp) and the HD-ONT workflow (nuclease and saponin host depletion, GridION R9.4.1). Reads were host-filtered against GRCh38 and classified against a curated database of 20,484 genomes or sequences. A species was called when normalised reads passed RP20M of at least 3 (short read) or RP10K of at least 1 (HD-ONT).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, NGS and TGS workflows; Bioinformatic processing; Reference database; Read normalization

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each workflow's organism calls are compared with three references: routine culture; clinical microbiological tests (culture plus qPCR or GeneXpert verification where residual volume allowed); and a composite reference standard that adds organisms detected by both sequencing workflows. Agreement is assessed per organism and summarised as PPA and NPA, restricted to bacteria and fungi. Against the composite standard, the paper reports PPA of 93.3% (NGS) and 90.7% (TGS), and NPA of 77.6% and 83.3%.

profile.summary: The evaluation from the BERTax paper: assign 1,500 nt genome fragments to superkingdom, phylum and, in one dataset, genus. BERTax is compared with Kraken2, sourmash, MMseqs2, minimap2 and DeepMicrobes, all given the same reference or training data, on a closely related split and a genus-held-out split. sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well a method assigns the taxonomic origin of a DNA fragment when close relatives are, or are not, in the reference data. The distantly related dataset simulates unknown sequences by holding out whole genera.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Genomes of archaea, eukaryotes, bacteria and viruses were taken from NCBI, and 1 million 1,500 nt fragments per superkingdom were extracted, then clustered at 80% identity. Fine-tuning data keep phyla with at least 10,000 fragments: 30 phylum classes and 2,328,584 samples. The closely related dataset tests on 2,000 random samples per phylum; the distantly related dataset tests on whole held-out genera, balanced to 1,780 samples per phylum; the final model dataset adds 2 million eukaryotic and bacterial fragments and has 5 superkingdom, 44 phylum and 156 genus classes, split like the closely related dataset. In every case 95% of the rest is training and 5% validation.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each tool is scored by macro average precision (AveP) at superkingdom and phylum, and at genus for the final dataset. Database tools get only the training partition as reference, default parameters are used, and MMseqs2 is also run with taxonomy parameters to obtain a confidence for precision-recall curves. DeepMicrobes is trained on the same data. The share of sequences each tool classifies is reported alongside, since database tools leave some unclassified.

profile.summary: These are the two clinical missense benchmarks from the ESM1b variant effect paper. One labels variants from ClinVar as pathogenic or benign; the other treats HGMD disease-causing variants as positives and gnomAD variants with allele frequency above 1% as negatives. Predictors are scored by a global ROC-AUC over all variants together, plus a class-balanced PRC-AUC, and only methods that avoid clinical-database training and allele frequency features are included in the main comparison.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b outperforms other VEP methods; Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a variant effect predictor separates harmful from harmless missense variants across the whole genome, not within one gene. The authors argue a global score matters because diagnosis means comparing variants in different genes, so the scores must be comparable between genes; they also report the gene-average ROC-AUC used by the EVE paper for contrast.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: ClinVar labels come from ClinVar's variant summary file, with only high-confidence variants kept. In the ESM1b versus EVE comparison the ClinVar set has 19,925 pathogenic and 16,612 benign variants across 2,765 genes, and the HGMD and gnomAD set has 27,754 disease-causing and 2,743 common variants across 1,991 genes; the paper does not say whether the full sets are larger. A separate ClinVar benchmark with EVE scores came from the EVE portal. Predictions for most of the compared methods were downloaded from dbNSFP 4.3a, with VARITY and MTBAN added separately. HGMD is a private resource, so that half of the benchmark cannot be redistributed.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods, Other VEP methods; Data availability; README.md: Data Availability

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Global ROC-AUC over the pooled variants is the main metric. The balanced PRC-AUC downsamples each dataset to an equal number of pathogenic and benign variants, taking 80% of the minority class, and averages over 100 such draws. Two comparison modes are reported: all 19 eligible methods on the variants that all of them score, and head-to-head comparisons where ESM1b is compared with each method on that method's own set of scored variants, with the percentage of variants used shown. Differences are tested by permutation, shuffling scores between variants over 2,000 iterations.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics and Testing for significant performance differences; Fig. 2 legend

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository holds the processed benchmark files with every method's predictions, except the HGMD variants, plus command line tools that score missense or multi-residue mutations with ESM1b. Install the dependencies, clone the repository, then run esm_score_missense_mutations.py on a FASTA file to get a score for every possible missense mutation.

profile.summary: This is the human variant effect evaluation in the Evo 2 paper, not a released benchmark suite. The authors scored ClinVar variants, SpliceVarDB splice variants and BRCA1 and BRCA2 functional assay variants zero-shot with Evo 2 and a range of comparison models, and report AUROC and AUPRC per variant stratum. It is useful for seeing how a DNA language model compares with conservation scores, protein language models and supervised predictors on coding, noncoding, SNV and non-SNV variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Human variant effect prediction, Fig. 3 legend; SI: A.3.12 to A.3.15

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model's zero-shot score separates harmful from harmless human variants. Four label sources are used: ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic versus benign or likely benign; SpliceVarDB experimentally validated splice-altering variants; BRCA1 saturation genome editing classes (loss of function versus functional or intermediate); and BRCA2 functional classifications. ClinVar results are split into coding and noncoding, SNV and non-SNV, by phyloP conservation bin and by distance from splice sites, so the evaluation also covers insertions, deletions and other non-SNVs that many predictors cannot score.
sections.source_locator: SI: A.3.13 to A.3.15; Paper: Human variant effect prediction

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: ClinVar is the October 2024 release, restricted to nuclear variants with at least two review stars, with variants of unknown significance removed and variants affecting more than 64 bp of reference or alternate sequence removed. SpliceVarDB variants labelled low frequency are excluded. BRCA1 and BRCA2 labels are the classes assigned in the original assay studies: for BRCA1, 823 loss-of-function SNVs against 3,070 functional or intermediate SNVs; for BRCA2, 1,156 against 5,681. All models score the same variants within each benchmark.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each variant is scored zero-shot as the change in log-likelihood between the variant and reference sequence; a more negative change means more deleterious. Evo 2 scores an 8,192 bp genomic window around the variant. Encoder models use masked marginal likelihood for SNVs and the change in pseudolikelihood for non-SNVs; PhyloP non-SNV scores average the affected positions; Pangolin uses the largest absolute predicted change in splice site usage. Classification is scored with AUROC and AUPRC per stratum. The full per-model, per-stratum results are in Supplementary Data 1. A separate supervised BRCA1 experiment trains ridge regression on Evo 2 embeddings with a position-grouped 80/20 split; it is not part of the zero-shot comparison.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: ClinVar October 2024 (coding: 14,319 SNVs and 1,236 non-SNVs; noncoding: 34,761 SNVs and 3,894 non-SNVs), SpliceVarDB (1,181 exonic and 3,769 intronic variants), BRCA1 saturation genome editing SNVs (3,893; 2,077 coding and 1,125 noncoding) and BRCA2 functional SNVs (1,156 loss of function and 5,681 functional or intermediate).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 3 legend; SI: A.3.15

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train or test split for the zero-shot comparison: all variants are evaluation data. The separate supervised BRCA1 experiment splits 1,326 genomic positions 80/20 into 3,104 training and 789 test SNVs.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC and AUPRC per stratum; higher is better.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: PhyloP (100, 241, 447 and 470 way), ESM models, Nucleotide Transformer, CodonBert, Decodon, EnCodon, RNA-FM, AlphaMissense, GPN-MSA, SpliceAI, Pangolin and CADD, each on the strata it can score.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: No variant-level control is described for comparison models. For Evo 2, the authors state it was not trained on human genetic variation or functional genomics data. Supervised comparators such as CADD, SpliceAI and Pangolin may have been trained on overlapping labels; the sources do not address this.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Human variant effect prediction, final paragraph

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Unreported: the sections read give point AUROC and AUPRC values without confidence intervals or replicates.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A human genetic variant (SNV, insertion, deletion or multi-nucleotide variant).

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Clinical classifications (ClinVar), experimentally validated splicing effects (SpliceVarDB) and functional scores from BRCA1 saturation mutagenesis and BRCA2 experimental measurements.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Human variant effect prediction; SI: A.3.15

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA models read the genomic sequence around the variant; protein models read the gene's amino acid sequence; conservation and supervised predictors use their own inputs.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot likelihood scoring for the main comparison; one supplementary experiment trains a ridge regression probe on Evo 2 embeddings for BRCA1.

strengths.text: Covers non-SNV variants (insertions, deletions, multi-nucleotide variants) as well as SNVs, and noncoding as well as coding regions.
Within each benchmark all models score the same variants, and ClinVar results are stratified by conservation and splice-site distance.
Uses functional assay labels (BRCA1, BRCA2, SpliceVarDB) alongside clinical labels.

limitations.text: It is one paper's evaluation, run by the Evo 2 authors. No scoring code for the full comparison is listed in the availability statements, only the Evo 2 repository with an example BRCA1 notebook. profile.summary: The variant effect benchmarks used in the GPN-MSA paper to test unsupervised deleteriousness scores on the human genome. They pit ClinVar pathogenic, COSMIC frequent and OMIM regulatory variants against common gnomAD variants, test enrichment of rare over common gnomAD variants among the most deleterious scores, and add ProteinGym DMS and DepMap gene essentiality. They are for comparing DNA language models with conservation scores, CADD and protein models on coding and non-coding variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Main VEP metrics

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a score ranks deleterious human variants above neutral ones without being trained on human variant labels. Coding variants are tested through ClinVar, COSMIC and DMS; non-coding through OMIM regulatory variants and gnomAD; gene-level through DepMap essentiality.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: ClinVar release 20230730; COSMIC MutantCensus v98 with frequency computed from whole-genome or whole-exome samples; a curated OMIM set of pathogenic regulatory variants; gnomAD 3.1.2 filtered to allele number of at least 25000 with common variants above 5% MAF and rare variants as singletons; ProteinGym v0.1 human DMS data; DepMap Public 23Q4 gene dependency. OMIM variants are matched to gnomAD common variants by regulatory category. The ablation set subsamples rare variants to match common variants per consequence. The labelled ClinVar, COSMIC, OMIM and gnomAD sets are published on Hugging Face.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, VEP data sources, Main and Additional VEP metrics; docs/models/gpn-msa.md

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each method gives one score per variant (for GPN-MSA, the log-likelihood ratio of alternate to reference, averaged over strands). ClinVar is scored by AUROC; COSMIC, OMIM and DepMap by AUPRC; gnomAD by the odds ratio of rare to common variants in the deleterious tail, with the tail set by allowing about 30 false discoveries and p-values from a one-sided Fisher's exact test. DMS sets are binarised with ProteinGym cut-offs, except TADBP, where a 0.125 cut-off on absolute relative toxicity is used. Some expensive models were scored only on ClinVar or part of OMIM.

review.method_note: Independent review pass of 2026-11-16. All four pinned artifacts were re-retrieved. The Nature article PDF, the Supplementary Information PDF and the Hugging Face collection API JSON each hashed to the value on their source record. The bioRxiv PDF did not and cannot: two downloads minutes apart gave b3e4d729d3363c16fb6b6cb99e4e18ffadb01b48614dba910480fb96f42b3d73 and 47f87f72baf93793177d3e40f70f43f03ac5d3050bbc5244f655e92041c7db4a, differing from each other in 34 bytes, all of them download-time stamps (XMP ModifyDate and MetadataDate, the xmpMM DocumentID and InstanceID, the document /ModDate and the second element of the trailer /ID); the page count, the CreationDate of 2025-09-21 and the pdftotext -layout text layer are identical across downloads. No value in this batch comes from the preprint. npm run batch -- check-values reproduced the extractor's figures exactly: 12 in_cell, 44 in_row, 16 locator_not_parsed, no not_in_row, no wrong_column and no overclaimed_in_row (value-check.tsv). All 72 results were then re-read by review/check_values_independent.py, written for this pass and importing nothing from extract/build.py. Supplementary Table 3 is printed rotated, so that script reads the page's word bounding boxes rather than a text dump: it recovers the seven column bands from the header words' y extents, pairing each 'Finemapped' header with whichever of 'coding' and 'non-coding' overlaps it, clusters the body words into eight row bands by x centre, and places every numeric token in the cell whose column centre is nearest, rejecting any token that is more than 45 per cent of a column pitch from its nearest column or less than 25 per cent of a pitch clear of the runner-up. Column order is therefore a measured property of the page and not an assumption, which is the check extract/build.py could not make: it asserted the column order positionally. Results are matched to cells through each source_locator's text, not through record IDs. Fig. 4b's 12 bar labels were required to be the first number printed after their series label on the same line, and the four rare variant counts were matched against the two sentences that print them, with the capture position fixing which count belongs to DeepRVAT with GPN-Star annotations and which to the original method. Result: 68 in cell, 4 in sentence, 0 failures (review/value-check-independent.tsv). Two negative controls confirm the checker is a cell check and not a row check: exchanging two ClinVar values between rows and moving a Fig. 4b label onto another series both fail (review/control-swap.tsv), and shifting a value into a neighbouring column of its own row fails and names the column that actually holds it, including across the Finemapped coding / OMIM and Finemapped coding / Finemapped non-coding boundaries (review/control-shift.tsv). Independently of both scripts, all 56 cells of Supplementary Table 3 and all 12 Fig. 4b labels were transcribed by hand from the pages rendered at 190 dpi with pdftoppm, into review/manual-transcription.tsv, and compared by review/cmp_manual.py: 68 values, 0 problems. That hand pass is what settles the column assignment the repository checker could only place at row level. The 12 descriptive claims were read against the pinned PDFs and the collection JSON.

name: CACHE Challenge #3
description: Blinded prospective community challenge in which computational teams select commercially available compounds for a named target, the organisers synthesise and assay them, and confirmed hits are scored by an independent Hit Evaluation Committee.

attributes.task: Prospective hit identification for the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3 macrodomain (Mac1)
attributes.scope_note: Round 1 (hit identification): each of 23 workflows selected up to 100 commercially available compounds; 1739 were synthesised by Enamine and tested. All 1739 were screened at 100 uM by homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF); 302 reduced the binding signal by 30% or more in at least one of two duplicates or gave ambiguous data and went to a limited three-point dose response, then to surface plasmon resonance; 28 advanced to Round 2. In parallel all 1739 were soaked with crystallised Nsp3-Mac1, giving complex structures for 44. Round 2 (hit expansion): up to 50 close analogues per team, 296 compounds tested, 84 confirmed. Teams were also asked to predict actives from the merged library of all 1739 Round 1 compounds, so that every workflow ran on the same library; confirmed hits with a score above 15 were clustered into four chemically novel Tier 1 compounds and 25 Tier 2 compounds.
attributes.source_locator: Results 'Compounds Were Drug-like and Chemically Diverse', 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging', 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'; Figure 6 caption
limitations: The challenge scores confirmed hits with an activity score set by a Hit Evaluation Committee and a novelty score voted by three chemists. It does not publish a per-workflow hit rate.

Targets and libraries were chosen by the organisers and predictions were submitted before testing, so there is no training-overlap control in the usual sense; the Nsp3-Mac1 binding features were already well documented, and 61 Mac1 ligands had been published.
Only the published CACHE #3 round is extracted here. The CACHE #1 and #2 results papers (doi 10.1021/acs.jcim.4c01267 and 10.1021/acs.jcim.5c00535) are not open access and were not retrieved.

profile.summary: DNALONGBENCH is five DNA prediction tasks that need long input sequences, up to about 1 million base pairs: enhancer-target gene pairs, eQTLs, 3D chromatin contact maps, regulatory sequence activity and base-pair transcription initiation signals. Each task compares a task-specific expert model, a CNN and fine-tuned DNA foundation models (HyenaDNA, Caduceus-Ph, Caduceus-PS). It is for developers testing whether long-context DNA models capture long-range dependencies.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model can use long DNA context for problems where distant sequence matters: linking enhancers to target genes, flagging eQTLs, predicting chromatin contacts, predicting thousands of epigenomic tracks, and predicting transcription initiation at base-pair resolution.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Proposed dataset

sections.title: Enhancer-target gene and eQTL tasks
sections.body: Enhancer-target gene pairs are CRISPRi-validated enhancer-promoter interactions in K562 cells from three studies, kept within 450 kb of the TSS; 2,602 samples, scored by AUROC. The eQTL task adapts Enformer's SuSiE fine-mapped eQTL set for the top nine tissues, keeps candidates within 450 kb of the TSS, masks other variants in each interval, and splits 8:1:1 by stratified random sampling; 31,282 samples, scored by AUROC.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods; README.md: Data Download table

sections.title: Contact map, regulatory activity and transcription initiation tasks
sections.body: Contact maps use Akita's processed data for five cell lines plus four more from the 4DN portal, 1 Mbp inputs at 2 kb bins, split by random virtual contigs 8:1:1 into 7008, 419 and 413 sequences, scored by SCC and PCC. Regulatory activity uses Enformer's 5313 human and 1643 mouse tracks, with 1937 human and 2017 mouse test sequences, scored by PCC averaged over test samples. Transcription initiation uses Puffin's data for five assays on both strands, evaluated on test chromosomes 8 and 9 by PCC.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each task reuses processed data from earlier studies (CRISPRi screens, Akita, Enformer, Puffin) and provides inputs as BED coordinates so flanking context can be changed. The datasets are deposited on Harvard Dataverse.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Data availability

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are trained or fine-tuned on each task's training split and scored on its test set with the task's metric: AUROC for the two classification tasks, SCC and PCC for contact maps, PCC for the two regression tasks. Foundation models feed sequence features to linear heads; for eQTL, reference and alternate representations are combined before a classifier. The paper reports that expert models scored highest on every task.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Representative models; Methods; Discussion

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Create the conda environment, clone the repository and install the package, download a task's data from Dataverse, then run the CNN baseline's train.py for that task; the script trains, saves the best validation checkpoint to best_model.pt, and prints the test metric for the final-epoch model, not the saved checkpoint.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Experiments; experiments/CNN/README.md; train.py

strengths.text: Covers several long-range genomic problems with different output types: classification, binned 1D and 2D regression, and base-pair regression.
Inputs are given as BED coordinates, so the flanking context can be changed without reprocessing.
Data are on Harvard Dataverse under CC0 1.0 and the code is BSD-3-Clause, with a Zenodo archive of the published version.
strengths.source_locator: Dataverse records; Paper: Code availability; LICENSE

limitations.text: Transformer foundation models such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer were not evaluated because of their compute cost on long inputs.
Expert models were each designed and trained for their task, and ABC uses extra experimental inputs, so expert and sequence-only scores are not like-for-like.
Several splits are random (contact map contigs, eQTL pairs), and no uncertainty estimates are reported in the text read.
Most task data are reprocessed from earlier studies (Akita, Enformer, Puffin) rather than newly generated.

The CNN baseline's train.py saves the best validation checkpoint to best_model.pt but never reloads it: the test metric it prints comes from the model after the last epoch, not from the best validation epoch.

name: GenBench
description: Benchmark suite of short- and long-range genomic tasks for fine-tuned genomic foundation models.

attributes.task: Genomic sequence classification and regression
attributes.scope_note: Tables 3-8 and 10.
attributes.source_locator: Tables 2-10

profile.summary: GenBench is a benchmark suite and codebase for genomic foundation models. It gathers forty-three datasets covering coding regions, non-coding regions and genome architecture, split into short-range tasks (inputs under 1,000 bases) and long-range tasks, and runs ten models through the same fine-tuning framework. Tasks include sequence classification, token classification and regression, scored by accuracy, AUC-ROC, Pearson or Spearman correlation and mean squared error depending on the task.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Sections 3.1 to 3.4; README.md: Introduction

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The suite is organised around three parts of the genome: the coding region, the non-coding region and genome architecture. Short-range tasks, with inputs under one thousand bases, cover enhancers, promoters, transcription factor binding, splice sites, epigenetic marks, open chromatin, species discrimination and SARS-CoV-2 variant classification. Long-range tasks cover splice site annotation, species classification, promoter prediction, bulk RNA expression across 218 tissue types and genomic structure prediction. The paper's stated aim is to see whether attention-based and convolution-based models differ in where they do well.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 1, 3.2 and 3.3

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The datasets are taken from earlier published collections rather than created: the Genomic Benchmarks tasks (mouse enhancers, coding versus intergenomic, human versus worm, enhancers, regulatory regions, non-TATA promoters, open chromatin), the GUE tasks (promoters, transcription factor binding, splice sites, yeast epigenetic marks, SARS-CoV-2 variants), the GENA-LM long-range tasks (splice sites, promoters, Drosophila enhancer activity), genomic structure prediction from Orca and species classification from HyenaDNA. Table 2 lists each task's type, training and test size and input length, from 30 bases for transcription factor prediction up to 256 Mb for genomic structure. For practicality the authors limited genomic structure prediction to 6,000 bases and capped long sequence tasks at 30 kb in their own experiments.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.3 and 4, Table 2; README.md: supported datasets

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are fine-tuned within the suite's own framework, which loads pretrained weights from Hugging Face, so every model goes through the same pipeline. Metrics are chosen per task: cross-entropy as the error for classification and mean squared error for regression; top-1 accuracy and AUC-ROC for classification; Spearman and Pearson correlation for regression. Parameter count and floating point operations are also reported as computational measures. The published tables report top-1 accuracy for the short-range tasks, AUC-ROC for long-range splice site prediction, Pearson for Drosophila enhancer activity and genomic structure, and Spearman with MSE for bulk RNA expression.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.4, 3.5 and 4, Tables 3 to 8

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The codebase is organised into a core layer, an algorithm layer and a user interface layer, with configuration files per experiment. Create the conda environment from the shipped file, install the package, then run train.py with an experiment configuration, a dataset name and the path to a pretrained model. Each supported dataset has its own download link and configuration directory in the README.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation, Getting Started; Paper: Section 3.5

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Forty-three datasets, grouped in Table 2 into twenty-one benchmark tasks: eight Genomic Benchmarks tasks at 500 bases, eight GUE and DeepSTARR short-range tasks from 30 to 256 bases, and five long-range tasks (splice site prediction at 15 kb, species classification at 80 Mb, promoters prediction at 8 kb, genomic structure at 256 Mb and bulk RNA expression at 196 kb). Test sizes run from 3 examples for genomic structure to 57K for human Ensembl regulatory regions.

strengths.text: Covers both short and long inputs, with tasks up to the hundreds of kilobases, which the authors say earlier benchmarks either avoided or reduced to classification.
All ten models run through one modular codebase with per-experiment configuration files, released under Apache 2.0.
Task types go beyond classification to token-level classification and regression, including two-value regression for Drosophila enhancer activity and 218-dimensional bulk RNA output.

limitations.text: The authors state GenBench covers only downstream task prediction, with no comparison of pretraining choices, and that they did not test whole-chromosome performance because of compute limits.

Sequence lengths were cut for practicality: genomic structure prediction was limited to 6,000 bases and long sequence tasks were capped at 30 kb, so the stated input lengths in Table 2 are not what was run.
No leakage control is described, so a model pretrained on the human genome may have seen the test sequences as unlabelled data.
Some test sets are very small: three examples for genomic structure prediction, 242 for mouse enhancers and 500 for species classification.

name: GENEB leaderboard
description: Frozen-embedding probing benchmark of genomic foundation models over 100 tasks in 13 categories, with full-data, 10-shot and 1-shot regimes.

attributes.task: Genomic sequence classification from frozen embeddings
attributes.scope_note: MCC aggregates only: micro average over all 100 tasks, macro average (unweighted mean of the 13 category MCCs), and per category.

profile.summary: GENEB compares 40 genomic foundation models on 100 DNA sequence classification tasks in 13 functional categories, such as promoters, enhancers, histone marks, DNA methylation and splice sites. Every model is scored the same way: a logistic-regression probe trained on frozen sequence embeddings, in full-data, 10-shot and 1-shot regimes, with MCC as the main metric. It is meant for choosing a DNA model for a particular kind of task rather than for a single overall ranking.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs and Benchmark table; Paper: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: GENEB tests how much task-relevant information a pretrained DNA model's frozen embeddings carry. Tasks are binary or multi-class sequence classification problems in 13 categories: histone modifications (30 tasks), promoters (22), enhancers (8), DNA methylation (8), splice sites (7), lncRNA (6), mouse enhancers (5), TF binding (5), species classification (3), regulatory elements (2), virus or phage (2), coding versus non-coding (1) and chromatin accessibility (1). The authors argue that rankings change across categories and data regimes, so results are reported per task and per category as well as overall.
sections.source_locator: benchmark_spec.json: categories; README.md: opening note

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The tasks are taken from nine earlier benchmark collections: the original and revised Nucleotide Transformer tasks, GUE, Genomic Benchmarks, the Plant Genomic Benchmark, iPro-WAEL, deep4mc, iDNA-ABF and iDHS-EL. Each task is one CSV with a sequence, a label and a train or test split. The released train and test partitions of the source benchmarks are used as published, without relabelling or resplitting. Tasks with more than 10^5 sequences are subsampled. The task data are pinned to one Hugging Face dataset revision in benchmark_spec.json.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix B; README.md: Evaluation protocol; benchmark_spec.json: dataset

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is an embedding extractor that turns each DNA sequence into one fixed-length vector. The harness fits a logistic-regression probe (max_iter=1000) on the training embeddings and scores the test set, in three regimes: all training data, 10 examples per class and 1 example per class. Results are averaged over five fixed seeds (13, 17, 42, 123, 997). MCC is the primary metric; accuracy and macro-F1 are also reported. The leaderboard gives a micro average over all 100 tasks and a macro average, the unweighted mean of the 13 category scores. Encoders must not be fine-tuned on task labels. Evaluation is run by the contributor; continuous integration checks the submission file but does not recompute embeddings, and community entries are marked self-reported.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3 Probing setup; README.md: Evaluation protocol, Leaderboard; run_GENEB.py: few_shot_idx; CONTRIBUTING.md: What CI verifies

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Download the pinned task data with the repository's sync tool, write an extractor class for your model under harness/extractors/, run harness/run_GENEB.py (the README suggests --limit 5 for a smoke test) and validate the submission file it writes. The README commands use placeholder names for the extractor and model.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Evaluate your model; CONTRIBUTING.md: Quick start

strengths.text: Every model is run on the full task suite under one probe protocol, which the authors say allows matched comparisons across architecture, tokenisation and pretraining data.
Results are reported per task and per category, and in three data regimes, not only as one aggregate.
The task data revision is pinned in the benchmark definition, and the harness, submissions and leaderboard build are public.

limitations.text: Results are self-reported: maintainers do not re-run submissions, and CI only checks the file format and ranges.
Splits are inherited from the source benchmarks and no check for overlap with pretraining data is made, so some models may have seen test sequences during pretraining.

limitations.text: Few tasks need long-range context beyond 10 kb, and 12 of the 13 categories are eukaryotic; the authors also say some constituent tasks may be noisy or weakly defined.
The Apache-2.0 licence covers the code only; the task data keep the terms of their upstream sources, which the files read do not list.

attributes.source_locator: Technical Methods; Appendix task descriptions; Tables 1-5

profile.summary: GFMBench-API is a Python interface that puts many existing genomic benchmarks behind one evaluation API. A model implements a small set of inference methods, and the library then runs it on 22 tasks covering supervised sequence and variant classification and zero-shot variant effect prediction, writing one CSV of task and metric rows. It is for comparing genomic foundation models without rewriting a pipeline per benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening, Supported Benchmarks & Tasks, Benchmark Output

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two families of task. Supervised classification and variant prediction: promoter, splice site and transcription factor binding from GUE; coding, non-coding, expression, common versus rare, methylation QTL and splicing QTL variant classification from VariantBenchmarks; causal eQTL, enhancer and histone mark tasks from the Long Range Benchmark. Zero-shot variant effect prediction: ClinVar SNVs by embedding distance and by likelihood, ClinVar insertions and deletions, BEND expression and disease effects, BRCA1 functional impact, TraitGym complex and Mendelian variants, LRB pathogenic OMIM variants and LOL-EVE causal eQTL indels.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Supported Benchmarks & Tasks

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The tasks wrap data from existing benchmarks rather than new data collection. All task data sit under one root directory, one subdirectory per task named after the task class, holding train.csv, dev.csv and test.csv; missing files are downloaded automatically on first use. Classification data carry a sequence and a label; variant effect data carry a reference sequence, an alternative sequence and a label. Sequences use A, T, C, G, N and P for padding at chromosome boundaries, and are upper-cased. The NOTICE states that the downloaded third-party data include datasets with non-commercial terms.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Data Preparation; NOTICE

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model supplies inference methods by duck typing: sequence to label probabilities, variant and reference pairs to label probabilities, sequence to regression outputs, sequence to per-nucleotide probabilities and embeddings, a position mapping helper, and masked-position token probabilities. Any method a model does not implement can return None and the metrics that need it are skipped. Supervised classification tasks compute accuracy, MCC, AUROC and AUPRC. Zero-shot SNV tasks add cosine similarity AUROC and AUPRC between variant and reference embeddings at the variant position, and AUROC and AUPRC on the masked-token log-likelihood ratio. Tasks expose eval_test_set, eval_validation_set and eval_cross_validation_fold, and results go to a CSV with one row per task and metric and one column per model name, with NO_RESULTS where a result is missing.
sections.source_locator: README.md: How Model & Task Interfaces Work, Benchmark Output; base task classes

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install your model's own dependencies first, then the library's basic_requirements.txt on top, and run usage_examples/run_benchmark.py with a model key. Flags select linear probing, the number of fine-tuning epochs, the output CSV path and the inference cache size. A sanity check mode runs on 100-sample subsets. If a model's dependencies clash with the benchmark stack, the model can run in a separate Python environment and process behind a thin adapter.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Quick Start, Example: Running Benchmarks

facts.value: 22 tasks wrapping data from GUE, VariantBenchmarks, the Long Range Benchmark, BEND, TraitGym, the SongLab ClinVar set, BRCA1, VEP-eval, LOL-EVE and a ClinVar indel task. The README gives no example counts per task.

description: Genome Understanding and ANnotation in silico Evaluation, version 1.1: functional genomics, conservation, gene-expression and variant tasks on hg38.

attributes.task: Regulatory sequence, conservation, expression and variant-effect prediction
attributes.scope_note: Tasks in this batch: dnase-propensity, ccre-propensity, cons30, cons100, gpra-c, gpra-d (Table 2), cadd-snv (Table 3), clinvar-snv (Table 4).
attributes.source_locator: Abstract; Table 1; Tables 2-4

profile.summary: GUANinE v1.1 is a set of large genomic prediction tasks on the human reference genome hg38 and synthetic yeast promoters: chromatin accessibility and regulatory element propensity, sequence conservation, promoter expression, and two variant tasks for deleteriousness (cadd-snv) and pathogenicity (clinvar-snv). Pretrained models are compared with frozen features and a linear probe, scored by Spearman's rho. It suits people comparing supervised sequence-to-function models with genomic language models.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Introduction; v1.0 paper Table 1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Six tasks from v1.0 cover three domains with two tasks each: regulatory element annotation (dnase-propensity, ccre-propensity), sequence conservation (cons30, cons100) and expression of synthetic yeast promoters (gpra-c, gpra-d). Version 1.1 adds cadd-snv, which separates proxy-benign from proxy-deleterious variants, and clinvar-snv, which separates benign from pathogenic noncoding ClinVar variants. The authors say clinvar-snv is a splicing-rich subset of ClinVar, not a test of general pathogenicity.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Newly constructed tasks; Table 1 footnote

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: dnase-propensity labels 511 bp hg38 sequences with an ordinal score from 0 (inaccessible) to 4 (almost always accessible), aggregated from over 700 ENCODE SCREEN v2 DHS tracks; ccre-propensity relabels the positive DHSs by four epigenetic marks. cons30 and cons100 label 512 bp segments by binned mean phyloP30 or phyloP100 (0 to 24). gpra-c and gpra-d are 80 bp random yeast promoters labelled by binned fluorescence (0 to 17). cadd-snv uses gnomAD v3 singletons as proxy deleterious and simulated or frequent variants as proxy benign. clinvar-snv has no training set and just under 12 000 variants. Regulatory and variant tasks use chromosome 21 as development and chromosome 22 as test; conservation and yeast tasks use random splits.
sections.source_locator: v1.0 paper: Section 2 and Table 1; v1.1 paper: Table 1 and Newly constructed tasks; docs/tasks/dnase_propensity.rst

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are frozen; features are extracted and a linear probe (ridge or logistic regression) is fitted, with the regularisation chosen on the development set before test inference. clinvar-snv has no training set, so models that cannot score zero-shot are calibrated on the development set. Scores are Spearman's rho, reported multiplied by 100 in the documentation example. Most test labels are private; the README says test predictions are submitted through a Google form until an automatic evaluation server launches.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation methods; docs/scoring.rst; README.md: Submissions

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install Git LFS and the optional Python tools, clone a task dataset from Hugging Face, download hg38.2bit, extract sequences around each region centre, and score development-set predictions with scipy's spearmanr. Test-set scoring needs a submission to the maintainers.

strengths.text: Test sets are large (about 12 thousand to about a million examples per task), which the authors say allows well-powered model ranking.
Frozen-feature linear probing removes fine-tuning hyperparameters as a confounder, in the authors' view.
Private test labels for most tasks are meant to prevent accidental overfitting to the test set.
Covers both functional annotation and evolutionary conservation, plus two variant tasks.

limitations.text: Conservation and yeast promoter tasks use random splits, so nearby or related sequences can fall in both training and test sets.
No public leaderboard or automatic scoring: test predictions go to the maintainers through a Google form.
Supervised models trained on ENCODE tracks, including chromosome 22, may score inflated on the propensity tasks.
Licence terms vary by task: cadd-snv and cadd-indel derive from a modified MIT licence and commercial users may need a licence to release models built on them.

steps.title: Extract a sequence
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
import twobitreader

train_bed = pd.read_csv('dnase_propensity/bed/train/train.bed', sep='\t')

width  = 2000
chr    = train_bed.iloc[0]['#chr']
center = train_bed.iloc[0]['center']
start  = center - width//2
end    = center + width//2

hg38   = twobitreader.TwoBitFile('hg38.2bit')
sequence = hg38[chr][start:end]
print(chr, center, train_bed.iloc[0]['y'], sequence)
PY

name: Nucleotide Transformer benchmark (18 tasks)
description: Eighteen human genomic classification tasks (ten histone marks, enhancers, enhancer types, three promoter sets and three splice-site sets) scored by MCC with tenfold cross-validation.

attributes.task: Genomic sequence classification
attributes.scope_note: Probing (Supplementary Table 6) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (Supplementary Table 7) of NT models, with DNABERT-2, HyenaDNA, Enformer, BPNet and randomly initialised controls.
attributes.source_locator: Supplementary Table 5; Supplementary Tables 6, 7 and 9

profile.summary: The Nucleotide Transformer benchmark is a set of 18 human genomic classification tasks: ten histone marks in K562, three promoter tasks, two enhancer tasks and three splice site tasks. Each is a small balanced dataset of short sequences with a fixed chromosome-based test split, scored by Matthews correlation coefficient under tenfold cross-validation. The paper uses it to compare DNA language models after probing or fine-tuning, and the data are published on Hugging Face with an interactive leaderboard.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Methods, Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks; Supplementary Table 5; Hugging Face dataset record

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model's representation of a short DNA sequence carries the signal for a specific regulatory or structural feature. The ten epigenetic tasks ask whether a 1 kb sequence overlaps a histone mark peak in K562. The promoter tasks ask whether a 300 bp sequence contains a promoter, a TATA-box promoter or a promoter without a TATA box. The enhancer tasks ask whether a 400 bp sequence contains an enhancer, and in the multi-label version whether it is tissue-specific or tissue-invariant. The splice tasks ask whether a 600 bp sequence has an acceptor or donor site in the centre.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Histone marks come from ten ENCODE ChIP-seq narrowPeak files for K562, each identifier listed in the Methods. Promoters come from the Eukaryotic Promoter Database (29,598 regions, 3,065 of them TATA-box). Enhancers come from ENCODE SCREEN, with distal and proximal combined and tissue specificity from the Meuleman DHS index. Splice sites come from GENCODE V44, excluding level-3 automated annotations, extracted with the HISAT2 script. Sequences containing N are removed, each dataset is balanced by subsampling negatives to the number of positives, and the sets are then capped at 30,000 training and 3,000 validation and test examples so a new model can be benchmarked quickly. Supplementary Table 5 lists the resulting sizes per task, from 5,062 training sequences for Promoter non-TATA to 30,000 for most tasks.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Supplementary Table 5

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The split is by chromosome: chromosomes 20 and 21 are the test set and the rest is training. Evaluation uses tenfold cross-validation on the training set, training ten times with a different tenth held out for validation and checkpoint selection, and evaluating every run on the same held-out test set; the median across the ten folds is the reported performance. The metric is binary or multi-class MCC. For a single number per model, the authors take the median MCC within each of the three task categories (chromatin profiles, regulatory elements and splicing) and then the mean of those three.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

sections.title: Probing and fine-tuning
sections.body: The paper reports two ways of using a pretrained model. Probing stores embeddings from ten layers of the model and trains a downstream logistic regression or MLP on them, with a hyperparameter search of 100 trials guided by a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator and the same tenfold scheme; the authors say this produced 760,000 downstream models. Fine-tuning is parameter-efficient on the transformer part. A logistic regression on the tokenised sequence, before the transformer layers, is the raw baseline.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Probing

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The task data are published as a Hugging Face dataset, the revised version released after peer review, which the dataset card recommends using in place of the older one. The paper gives no command line pipeline for a third party to score a model, and results are collected in an interactive leaderboard on Hugging Face Spaces.
sections.source_locator: Hugging Face dataset record: description; Paper: Data availability

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 18 tasks. Ten histone marks (H2AFZ, H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K36me3, H3K4me1, H3K4me2, H3K4me3, H3K9ac, H3K9me3, H4K20me1) at 1 kb; Promoter all, TATA and non-TATA at 300 bp; Splice site all, donor and acceptor at 600 bp; Enhancer and Enhancer types at 400 bp. Training sets run from 5,062 to 30,000 sequences and test sets from 212 to 3,000, as Supplementary Table 5 prints them.
facts.source_locator: Supplementary Table 5

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Test is chromosomes 20 and 21; everything else is training, and the training set is further split tenfold for validation and checkpoint selection. Each dataset is class-balanced by subsampling negatives.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Matthews correlation coefficient, binary or multi-class depending on the task, higher is better; the median over the ten folds is reported per task.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Supplementary Table 5

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: A logistic regression on the tokenised sequence as a raw probe, BPNet at three sizes, and three published pretrained models: DNABERT-2, HyenaDNA at 1 kb and 32 kb context, and Enformer's torso. DNABERT-1 was excluded because its maximum input is 512 bp.

facts.value: The chromosome split is the only control: there is no sequence identity filter and no removal of homologous regions. The authors warn that Enformer was pretrained with different data splits, so its benchmark performance may be inflated by leakage.

facts.value: A short DNA sequence of fixed length (300, 400, 600 or 1,000 bp) with a binary or multi-class label.

strengths.text: Small, balanced and capped datasets, so a new model can be evaluated on all 18 tasks quickly.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

strengths.text: Tenfold cross-validation with a fixed held-out test set and a median across folds, rather than a single training run.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

strengths.text: The data are published on Hugging Face in a revised post-review version, with an interactive leaderboard for cross-model comparison.
strengths.source_locator: Hugging Face dataset record; Paper: Data availability

limitations.text: Short sequences and a chromosome split only; the paper describes no sequence identity or homology filtering and does not say whether the test chromosomes were in each model's pretraining data.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

limitations.text: Two of the comparison models are not on equal footing: Enformer was trained supervised with different splits, which the authors say may inflate its score, and HyenaDNA was fully fine-tuned while the others were not.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Comparison with published pre-trained genomics models

limitations.text: Some test sets are small (212 sequences for Promoter non-TATA, 776 for H3K4me3), so differences on those tasks rest on few examples.
There is no released evaluation harness: the data and a leaderboard are public, but the paper describes no command line pipeline for a third party to score a model the same way.
